extracted.intended_audience: educational psychologists, researchers of learning and emotion, instructors and graduate students in educational psychology
extracted.subtask_description: The article outlines theoretical (control–value) and empirical criteria for studying students' academic emotions, their antecedents, effects on learning/self-regulation/achievement, measurement (AEQ and related scales), and instructional/intervention implications. It guides design, measurement, and interpretation of research in this domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion classification by valence and activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify academic emotions along the dimensions of valence (positive vs. negative) and activation (activating vs. deactivating) when analyzing their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses original framing such as 'positive activating emotions', 'negative activating emotions', and 'negative deactivating emotions'. Examples: enjoyment, hope, pride (positive activating); relaxation, boredom (deactivating); anger, anxiety, shame (negative activating). The classification predicts different impacts on motivation, strategy use, and achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic versus extrinsic emotions (task-related vs. setting-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish emotions that are intrinsic to the task/material (relating to inherent properties of task material or the process) from extrinsic emotions relating to setting, other persons, or the self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states intrinsic positive emotions (e.g., task-related enjoyment, flow) are more likely to direct attention toward the task and facilitate learning, whereas extrinsic emotions may produce task-irrelevant thinking and distract cognitive resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on motivation (intrinsic and extrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how specific emotions influence intrinsic motivation (interest/enjoyment) and extrinsic motivation (outcome-related efforts), including ambivalent effects of activating negative emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General assumptions: positive activating emotions strengthen intrinsic motivation; negative deactivating emotions (boredom, hopelessness) reduce intrinsic motivation; negative activating emotions (anger, anxiety, shame) may reduce intrinsic but strengthen certain extrinsic motivations (e.g., avoidance). Empirical correlations in studies (e.g., enjoyment correlated positively with study interest and effort) illustrate these patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on learning strategies (flexible vs. rigid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether emotions facilitate flexible, creative strategies (elaboration, organization, critical evaluation, metacognitive monitoring) versus rigid strategies (simple rehearsal, algorithmic procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive academic emotions are assumed to facilitate flexible strategies; negative emotions tend to trigger rigid strategies. Effects should be expected to be stronger for activating than deactivating emotions. Empirical findings: positive emotions related positively to metacognitive strategies and elaboration; some negative activating emotions (anger, anxiety, shame) in some datasets related to increased rehearsal use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on cognitive resources and task-irrelevant thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how emotions consume or free cognitive resources and their propensity to produce task-irrelevant thoughts that impair performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotions direct attention toward the object of emotion and can distract attention away from tasks. While many emotions (enjoyment, pride, admiration, anxiety, anger, envy) can produce task-irrelevant thinking, intrinsic task-related enjoyment and flow may focus attention and allow full use of cognitive resources. The article references use of scales assessing task-irrelevant thinking (adapted from Sarason, 1984).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulation versus external regulation of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate relations between emotions and learners' perceived regulation source: self-regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating) versus external regulation by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive academic emotions correlate with perceived self-regulation; negative emotions correlate with perceived external regulation. Implication: fostering positive emotions may support self-regulated learning, whereas negative emotions may increase reliance on external guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicted effects on academic achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Link specific emotion types to expected effects on achievement, noting complexity and ambivalence (not all positive are beneficial and not all negative are harmful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary assumptions: positive activating emotions generally affect achievement positively (especially intrinsic enjoyment); negative deactivating emotions like boredom and hopelessness are generally detrimental; effects of positive deactivating and negative activating emotions are equivocal and context-dependent (e.g., anxiety sometimes related to extrinsic avoidance and weakly predictive of achievement). Empirical finding: positive emotions predicted higher achievement in longitudinal analyses except relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of validated measurement instruments (AEQ and complementary scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure academic emotions and related constructs with validated self-report instruments and performance indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends the Academic Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ; trait and state versions), German Study Interest Scale, motivated strategies for learning questionnaires (adaptations of Pintrich et al.), scales assessing task-irrelevant thinking (from Sarason), and objective indicators such as grades and written exam performance. The codebook and technical report for AEQ are referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research design recommendations: combine methods and temporal designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods and include cross-sectional, longitudinal, and diary/idiographic approaches to capture complexity and causal patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on qualitative or quantitative strategies; start with exploratory qualitative work to inform measures, then use sample-based quantitative testing. Use idiographic (within-person diary) analyses alongside nomothetic (between-person) analyses to test generalizability and detect heterogeneity (e.g., anxiety–motivation relations differ across individuals). Longitudinal and predictive designs are recommended for causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control–value theory as source-modeling criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt control-related and value-related appraisals as primary antecedent constructs when modeling sources of academic emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory posits that subjective control and subjective value interact and are necessary antecedents for most academic emotions. Control cognitions include self-efficacy, situation outcome, and action-outcome expectations; values include intrinsic and extrinsic valuations of learning and outcomes. Time perspective (retrospective, concurrent, prospective) should be considered in measuring appraisals. Empirical analyses should measure and test interactions of control and value variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom and social-environment antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate instructional and social variables that influence students' control and value appraisals and thereby their emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key environmental variables: (a) quality dimensions of classroom instruction (teacher enthusiasm), (b) autonomy support vs. control of students' learning, (c) achievement expectancies and values conveyed by significant others and classroom structures (competition vs. cooperation), (d) feedback and consequences of achievement (including career implications), (e) social relatedness and support (affiliation, teacher/parent/peer responses). Empirical work should measure these variables and test mediational paths through control/value appraisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional and intervention design guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Design instruction and interventions to modify control/value appraisals and foster beneficial emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists inferred guidelines: (a) improve instructional quality; (b) give students autonomy proportionate to their self-regulation ability; (c) convey high values of academic mastery but align social expectations with capabilities; (d) increase opportunities for success via individual and cooperative reference norms and promote learning from errors; (e) create flexible interaction structures that foster affiliation and cooperation without denying competition. Individual prevention/therapy can include attributional retraining to enhance perceived control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reciprocal causation and feedback loops
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting relationships among emotions, achievement, and antecedents, model bidirectional effects and potential positive/negative feedback loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotions influence achievement and achievement feedback influences emotions; emotions can also shape instructional environments via emotional contagion. Empirical designs should test for reciprocal causation (e.g., longitudinal cross-lag designs) and consider mechanisms such as emotional contagion and negative/positive feedback explaining counterintuitive correlations (e.g., support–anxiety correlations near zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include emotional diversity beyond test anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the full range of students' academic emotions (positive and negative) rather than focusing predominantly on test anxiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes analyzing positive emotions (enjoyment, hope, pride, admiration, empathy) as well as negative ones, because positive emotions can be as representative and consequential as negative emotions for learning and well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiographic analysis to test individual heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement nomothetic sample statistics with idiographic (within-person) analyses to assess whether between-person patterns hold at the individual level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diary methods and intraindividual correlations can reveal heterogeneity (e.g., anxiety correlating negatively with motivation for some students but positively for others). Use combined idiographic–nomothetic strategies to preserve both individual validity and generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure components of self-regulated learning as mediators
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying emotion effects, measure components of self-regulated learning (motivation/interest, effort, learning strategies, cognitive resources, regulation) as potential mediators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article operationalized these components with scales for study interest, effort, elaboration, rehearsal, irrelevant thinking, and perceived self- vs external regulation, and used them to test associations and mediation between emotions and achievement. Reporting correlations and longitudinal predictive relations among these components is recommended.
